name: Luna 2 impact site
founder: USSR; now Russia as its continuing state
story: Luna 2 struck the Moon in 1959, the first human object to reach its surface, and the wreckage lies near 29 degrees north. The impact point is an estimate. The mission predates the 1967 treaty and its registration system. Under Article VIII, ownership of a landed object is not affected by its presence on a celestial body, so title stays with the USSR's continuing state, Russia. The ground around it belongs to nobody.

sources.t: Wikipedia: List of artificial objects on the Moon

name: Apollo 11, Tranquility Base
story: The Eagle descent stage has stood here since July 1969, with an American flag, instruments and the bootprints of Armstrong and Aldrin. The coordinates are NASA's, measured from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images. Under Article VIII the United States keeps jurisdiction and control over the hardware it registered, and ownership is unaffected by its being on the Moon. That covers the objects only. Article II bars any claim to the ground beneath them.

name: Apollo 17, Taurus-Littrow
story: The last crewed landing so far came down here in December 1972. The Challenger descent stage, a Lunar Roving Vehicle and a science package remain in the valley on the southeastern rim of Mare Serenitatis. Cernan and Schmitt covered 30 kilometres and took 110.52 kilograms of samples away. Under Article VIII the United States keeps jurisdiction and control over the hardware and still owns it. It holds no title to the valley.

name: Chang'e 4, Von Kármán crater
story: Chang'e 4 made the first soft landing on the Moon's far side on 3 January 2019, inside Von Kármán crater in the South Pole-Aitken Basin. The lander and the Yutu-2 rover are both still on the surface. Article VIII gives the state on whose registry an object is carried jurisdiction and control over it, which here means China. The landing gives China no title to the crater.

name: Chang'e 6, Apollo Basin
story: Chang'e 6 landed on the far side on 1 June 2024 in the southern mare of Apollo Basin. Its ascent stage carried samples back, and the return capsule reached Inner Mongolia on 25 June. The descent stage stayed behind. Under Article VIII China keeps jurisdiction and control over that hardware, and ownership is unaffected whether an object stays on the Moon or returns to Earth. Removing samples created no claim to the site.

name: Chandrayaan-3, Vikram lander
story: The Vikram lander touched down on 23 August 2023 at about 69 degrees south, and the Pragyan rover worked nearby for 12 days. Both remain at the site, which India calls Shiv Shakti point. Article VIII leaves jurisdiction and control over the two machines with India as the state of registry. A national name for a landing point carries no territorial effect, since Article II bars appropriation of the Moon by any means.

name: SLIM, near Shioli crater
story: Japan's Smart Lander for Investigating Moon landed near Shioli crater on 19 January 2024. Its last contact came on 29 April 2024, and JAXA declared the mission over on 23 August 2024. The spacecraft is silent but remains Japanese property. Article VIII keeps jurisdiction and control with the state of registry, and the article sets no end date tied to the life of a mission.

name: Luna 25 crash site
story: On 19 August 2023 a failed orbital manoeuvre put Luna 25 on a path into the Moon, two days before its planned landing near Boguslawsky crater. It hit the inner rim of a crater, and the coordinates mark the impact, well short of the intended site. Under Article VIII a wreck is still an object launched into space, so ownership of the debris stays with Russia, along with jurisdiction and control.

name: Shackleton crater and the lunar south pole
founder: Target region of NASA's Artemis and the China-Russia ILRS; no state holds it
story: Shackleton is a crater almost at the south pole, marking a target region and not a landing site. NASA's nine candidate Artemis III regions of October 2024 lie around the pole, and China's Chang'e 7 is planned for Shackleton's rim. The ILRS was announced in 2021. Article VIII protects hardware only, so nothing here yet falls under it. Article II bars any state from claiming the ground.

name: Blue Ghost Mission 1, Mare Crisium
founder: United States (Firefly Aerospace, a private company, on a NASA-backed mission)
story: Firefly Aerospace's lander came down in Mare Crisium near Mons Latreille in March 2025 and operated until 16 March. It belongs to a company, and Article VIII's ownership rule protects that title. Jurisdiction and control rest with the state on whose registry the object is carried. Article VI separately makes the United States responsible for authorising and supervising its companies in space, so private hardware still answers to a state.

name: Mars 3 lander
founder: USSR; now Russia as its continuing state
story: Mars 3 made a soft landing in Terra Sirenum in 1971, then stopped transmitting 110 seconds later. The coordinates are an estimate. It carried a small PrOP-M rover. The Outer Space Treaty was already in force when it landed. Under Article VIII ownership is unaffected by the lander's presence on Mars, so title and control pass to Russia as the USSR's continuing state.

name: Viking 1 lander, Chryse Planitia
story: Viking 1 landed in western Chryse Planitia on 20 July 1976, at 22.27 degrees north and 312.05 degrees east in NASA's figures, the first American lander on Mars. It still sits there, long silent. Under Article VIII the United States keeps jurisdiction and control and continues to own the machine, which the article says is unaffected by its being on a celestial body. Neither the plain nor the planet became American by the landing.

name: Curiosity, Bradbury Landing, Gale crater
story: Curiosity landed on Aeolis Palus inside Gale crater on 6 August 2012, and the coordinates mark that landing point. The rover has since driven 38.16 kilometres, as of 30 October 2026, so its position changes. Under Article VIII the United States keeps jurisdiction and control over the rover wherever it travels. Control follows the object as it moves, and no ground it crosses comes under US sovereignty.

name: Perseverance, Jezero crater
story: Perseverance landed in Jezero crater on 18 February 2021, at the point marked here, and has been driving and collecting rock samples since. Some sealed sample tubes were cached on the surface for a possible return mission. Article VIII covers those tubes as component parts of a US object, so the United States keeps jurisdiction and control over them while they lie on Mars. Ownership survives a return to Earth too.

name: Tianwen-1 lander and Zhurong rover, Utopia Planitia
story: China's Tianwen-1 lander set down in May 2021, and the Zhurong rover worked for 358 days before a planned hibernation on 18 May 2022, ahead of sandstorms and winter. Sources differ slightly on exact position. Both machines remain on the surface. Article VIII gives China, as the state of registry, jurisdiction and control over lander and rover, and China's ownership is unaffected by their presence on Mars.

name: InSight lander, Elysium Planitia
story: InSight landed in western Elysium Planitia on 26 November 2018 to study the planet's interior. Its last contact was on 15 December 2022, and NASA declared the mission over on 21 December. Its seismometer and heat probe remain in place. Under Article VIII a retired lander is still a US object, so jurisdiction, control and ownership stay with the United States though nothing there now responds.

name: Phoenix lander, Green Valley
story: Phoenix landed in Green Valley in Vastitas Borealis in 2008, the northernmost site on this list. It operated for 155 sols, and its last contact came on 2 November 2008. The lander is still there in the Martian arctic. Article VIII keeps jurisdiction and control with the United States as the state of registry, and ownership is unaffected by the object's presence on Mars. The site gives no claim over the polar plain.
